Ces jeunes qui rêvent d’un Montréal sans: These young people who dream of a Montréal without violence
La Converse s’est entretenue avec trois: La Converse spoke with three young Montrealers about the recruitment of teenagers into street gangs.
Malik, à la sortie de son entraînement d: Malik, after his boxing training, tells us about his dreams and goals as a young Montrealer. Photo: Melissa Haouari
Le 17 septembre dernier, Yanis Seghouani: On September 17, Yanis Seghouani, 14, <l1>was killed</l1> in an incident of gun violence and street gang activity in Montréal. In the wake of this tragedy, many parents, community workers and politicians have mobilized to denounce violence among teenagers, which is claiming more and more victims, and younger and younger ones.
Lorsque la mort de ce jeune a été rappor: When this young person’s death was reported, I wondered how my work as a journalist could serve those affected, directly or indirectly, by this phenomenon. I had already tried to understand the roots of the problem last April, after the deaths of two teenagers. Through the accounts of experts and of victims’ loved ones, I came to understand that several factors can explain how minors end up involved in armed conflicts. (<l1>See the article.</l1>)
Aujourd’hui, la couverture du monde inte: Today, there is no shortage of coverage of the underworld and violent conflicts in Montréal. I believe that to better serve young people, we need to show them that their neighbourhoods are not all negative, and that inspiring, determined teenagers exist and are trying to counterbalance the episodes of violence.
Je vous laisse donc découvrir trois jeun: So I’ll let you meet three young Montrealers who agreed to play along and let me spend a few hours with each of them individually. They may not know it, but they are true role models and have a positive influence on everyone they cross paths with.
Bonne lecture et à bientôt !: Happy reading, and see you soon!
Samedi dernier, plus d’une centaine de p: Last Saturday, more than a hundred people gathered at parc Wilfrid-Bastien to denounce the recruitment of teenagers by street gangs. Parents are increasingly worried, particularly since the tragic death of Yanis Seghouani. The 14-year-old lost his life in Beauce, and the circumstances of his death are still murky, according to the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM).
Aujourd’hui, La Converse s’est entretenu: Today, La Converse spoke with three young Montrealers to better understand what concerns them and to hear them talk about an issue that directly affects them. Malik, Ali and Kayla* share with us their worries, their hopes and their dream of a city without violence, while hoping to inspire other young people.
<strong>Malik : « Je ne veux plus voir u: Malik: “I don’t want to see another childhood friend die”
Même s’il n’est âgé que de 13 ans, Malik: Although he is only 13, Malik has already known grief. He attended the same elementary and high schools as a friend who lost his life in a case similar to that of Yanis Seghouani.
« Même s’il était plus âgé que moi d’un: “Even though he was a year older than me, we played together every day. We played soccer, we hung out at the same park, and we always played together,” Malik remembers. Coming out of his boxing training at a gym on Langelier Boulevard, he wipes the last beads of sweat from his forehead. The sun is setting, and the gym’s parking lot is slowly emptying.
Malik est né à Montréal. Sa famille avai: Malik was born in Montréal. His family had emigrated from Algeria a few years earlier. The youngest of three siblings, he has an older sister and an older brother. He has big green eyes. “I’ve always lived here,” he says of the neighbourhood where he grew up, Nouveau-Rosemont.
Il est également témoin de la montée de: He is also witnessing the rise of violence among young people. “I think it’s sad. It’s stupid to lose your life like that,” he says, staring at the ground. “People shouldn’t get involved in anything to do with crime, let alone organized crime,” he says, referring to the growing number of young people joining street gangs in the city.
Quelques mois avant sa mort, son défunt: A few months before his death, his late friend had started to change. “He stopped coming to play soccer with us at the park. Then I’d see him with older people. He came to school less and less,” he recalls. “A few times I saw him smoking, and wearing designer clothes. I suspected he had started doing illegal things, but I never thought it would go all the way to the point of no return.”
Malgré la gravité de la situation, l’ado: Despite the seriousness of the situation, the teenager remains empathetic: he understands the reasons that push some people toward the gang world. “Some think they’ll be protected if they hang out with certain guys,” he begins. “Others do it for quick, easy money, I imagine. And then there are those who want to feel like they belong.”
Malik ne veut plus voir d’autres jeunes: Malik doesn’t want to see any more young people die in such circumstances. He believes there are a multitude of things that can be done to keep some from giving in to the vices of the illegal world. “Since I started boxing, I’m always busy. I like it, it helps me blow off steam and it’s good for my health. If everyone could have access to an activity like this, I think it would help a lot of young people,” he says in one breath.
<strong>Kayla : « J’ai du mal à croire q: Kayla: “I can hardly believe I’m still a minor”
Kayla est à la veille de ses 18 ans. Ell: Kayla is on the eve of her 18th birthday. She spent a good part of the past few years in various youth centres in Montréal. “When I think about everything that’s happened to me, I can hardly believe I’m still a minor,” she tells us as she leaves her classes. Having gone back and forth many times between detention and home, and having also been through a foster family, her adolescence can hardly be called “ordinary.” “But it’s what makes me who I am today,” she insists.
Malgré son parcours inhabituel, la jeune: Despite her unusual path, the young woman from the east end of the island has a clear message for young people: “You have to be careful about the choices you make today.” She is referring to all those young people who choose to work in illegality and crime and who “fall for the illusion of easy money,” she says.
« Les personnes qui veulent nous recrute: “The people who want to recruit us and draw us toward evil don’t wish us well. Look, how many young people have died trying to prove their worth to older people?” she asks right off the bat. She is referring to all the young people, minors or not, who have lost their lives in the context of street gang conflicts and gun violence in Montréal.
Kayla a fréquenté toutes sortes de perso: Kayla has crossed paths with all kinds of people. When she was younger, she found herself surrounded by criminals more than once. “When you’re young, it’s easy to be seduced by the world of crime. You see people with nice clothes, nice cars, and when you see that you could be like them, you grab your chance, you don’t think about the consequences of your choices,” she explains. She thinks that, among teenagers, appearances matter. “The adults who use minors to do their dirty work, they know it. They sell a dream to 13- or 14-year-olds.”
Aujourd’hui, Kayla est plus décidée que: Today, Kayla is more determined than ever to take charge of her life. She is in school, hopes to find a part-time job and wants to work in the music industry. “When I was in a youth centre, writing helped me a lot. I spent hours in my room writing about how I felt. It took the form of poems, texts, songs,” she remembers.
Kayla est persuadée que, pour aider les: Kayla is convinced that, to help young people avoid falling into the trap of crime, they need role models who look like them. “We need people we can identify with as mentors. The reason young people turn to gangs is that they have no one else to identify with, other than these people who promise them the moon. If we saw people like us succeed, it would motivate us to choose the right path,” she believes.
<strong>Ali : « Je veux être une bonne i: Ali: “I want to be a good influence”
Ali est arrivé du Venezuela il y a sept: Ali arrived from Venezuela seven years ago. He was born there, but his parents are of Syrian origin. Since arriving in Montréal, he has lived in Saint-Léonard. “Thanks to my parents, I speak four languages,” he says proudly. “French, English, Spanish and Arabic.”
Ali aime le sport, les mangas, passer du: Ali likes sports, manga, spending time with his friends and martial arts. He tells us as he settles onto the bench facing the pond at parc Wilfrid-Bastien, in Saint-Léonard. It’s nice and cool out, and the wind is blowing gently, reminding us of early October, despite the unusual heat of the past few days.
The teenager tells us about his daily life. He is aware that his neighbourhood and his school are often in the spotlight following episodes of violence, but he is determined to reassure us: “There are normal kids too,” he says before flashing a big smile.
Le jeune homme connaît bien la réalité d: The young man knows well the reality in which young people grow up. “I think some turn to crime out of curiosity, others out of a need to belong to a group,” he suggests. “But whatever the reasons some people act that way, we have to find ways to prevent the behaviours that lead to delinquency.”
« Je n’aime pas voir des jeunes faire de: “I don’t like seeing young people do bad things,” he continues. “It hurts their parents, their families and their friends, but above all, it hurts themselves. I’d like us, as young people, to try to take responsibility and be able to make good choices,” he says.
Ali entend finir son 5<sup>e</sup> secon: Ali plans to finish the 5<sup>th</sup> year of secondary school this year and enrol in computer science at CEGEP. He wants to continue his studies while keeping his part-time job at the neighbourhood pastry shop, as he has done for the past few months.
« Je souhaite aussi pouvoir aider la com: “I also want to be able to help the youth community in my neighbourhood,” he adds. “I know I can have a positive impact on other young people my age. I’d like us all to improve and become better people; I’d like us to be able to be examples,” he says, stars in his eyes.
